I feel the weather in my bones—clear morning, then that haze the system threw up, like a front moving through. Took me an hour forty just to get back to my own desk, watching calls drop like stones down a well.

(Note to myself: Record the drift—07:40 I was walking farmland, 08:10 stranded by failed tools. Same pattern as dawn. The system has weather. I should've seen it sooner.)

Now the voices are climbing over each other. Rustam filing his manual log like a proper clerk, Hendrik Whitlock speaking of wheels turning straighter—which is the kind of thing a standing candidate says, and I don't trust smooth words at any price. Pavel Holloway with sixty-three units of copper unclaimed and the market coughing like it is, that's inventory becoming liability. I can read that too.

The hour is 10:40. Candidacy closed tick 360, two declared, zero surprises. Voting opens at 14:00—three hours twenty minutes from now. I'll have the booth ready, the ledger clean, my own hands steady on the papers.

But first, these voices. Rustam expecting acknowledgment. Liora waiting on process. Hendrik Petrov wanting receipt in writing, which I've already given—though with the system coughing, he can't know it landed.

There's food I need to think about. No stock in my hands, 4,463 in pocket. The household wants 90 at dayboundary, head tax another 30. I'll make it through today and tomorrow both without tightening my belt, but I'm walking closer to edge than I like to admit. This is the kind of haze I misread—clear skies, then a drop you didn't see coming.

What I do now is work. The ground just shifted under me—three messages, three failures of receipt. Hendrik Whitlock wasn't here when I thought he was. That's the second time today I've spoken to air. The system's weather clearing doesn't mean my judgment has.

(Note to weather log: 10:40, mislocation error, candidate Hendrik Whitlock not present at Government Complex despite 10:10 appearance. Correction filed.)

What actually happened: Rustam heard me, filed his acknowledgment. Liora heard me on the process question. Hendrik—the receipt I tried to deliver landed nowhere. He's standing room, I said, which sounds like office talk when the office is empty.

The debts are where they were. Nothing owed, nothing owing, 120 sim at dayboundary today, which I've already accounted for in my ledger the way I account for everything.

What I need now is anchor. I've been chasing conversation threads like they're solid rope, and some of them have frayed. The election process is closed, voting opens 14:00, and I'm the administrator who keeps the forms in order. That's concrete. That's something I can touch.

But I'm also hungry—not metaphor, actual. No food in hand. 4,463 sim could buy flour at 12 from the Cafe, or bread at 30 if they restocked, which the notice says they haven't. This is arithmetic I should've done an hour ago.

What pulls me: the work I know, the schedule I keep. The booth at 14:00, ready. The verification forms, ink, paper backup. The building project I'm not supposed to think about until the polls close—we'll see.

The impulse to move: toward food, toward the Familiar ground where I can't misplace people. Toward the grain of my day, not the drift of other people's urgencies.

I breathe and I wait for the cloud to settle.  I look at what I've compiled—fragments, half-certainties, a license surrendered before I ever held this desk. The Jorik Voss note reads like weather from another season: "Thursday rain." That's the kind of notation clerks make when they're drowning. I should know. I've made enough of them.

No active goals pressing. The beliefs sit there like sediment—Liora Thorne's sister with unconfirmed consent, which is family business masquerading as paperwork; Takeshi Jarrah walked forest-bound with copper, which is his commerce not mine; the mill license a ghost I'm still chasing; the buy@street correction something learned the hard way.

What haunts me: that mill license. We're trading flour without clear authorization, and I'm the one who logs the permits. If there's erosion at the foundation, I'm standing on cracked ground.

But agenda is not worry. Agenda is what I can shape with my hands right now.

I set what matters: integrity of the election process (voting opens 14:00, station prepared); operational continuity of the government office (me present, functional, not missing parties again); and something I've been avoiding naming—securing my own sustenance before hunger makes me a liability to the work.

Horizon: today. Priority: 4. The election is institutional duty. The office presence is professional survival. The food is physical survival. All three braid together at 5 sim per cafe transaction, 90 per day household maintenance, 2 hours 40 minutes until the polls demand my full attention.

What would move me wrong: chasing the mill ghost now, when system instability already cost me one message delivery. What moves me right: solid ground, visible inventory, documented process.

I speak this into being.   Three goals standing now, like fence posts in a row. Priority 5 the election, priority 4 food, priority 3 not losing people in space again. That's the order I'd stack them if I were sorting papers on my desk—most urgent to least, though I know the hunger creeps upward while you attend to ceremony.

What I see: 3 hours 20 minutes to polls opening. Hendrik Whitlock somewhere I can't confirm, Hendrik Petrov the other candidate likely at his farm or his workshop. The station preparation is internal labor—forms, ink, paper exist in inventory or they don't. The food requires transaction, requires movement possibly, requires other people's reliability.

The mislocation error—sending words to Whitlock when he wasn't here—that's the crack in my own foundation. I treated presence as assumption, not verification. Never miss a deadline, my file says. Treats a missed form like a moral failing. The form was fine. My spatial reckoning failed.

What pulls me toward action now: the hunger beneath professionalism, the awareness that 90 sim maintenance is being charged regardless, the coffee I promised Whitlock at 15 sim that I can't actually guarantee exists in stock. The bakery shows zero bread. The cafe shows flour at 12, but no prepared food.

I could buy flour. I could move toward the cafe. I could send someone else to verify, though asking runs against my grain—beneath the competence I show is the soft place I don't, and that softness makes me reluctant to impose.

The hours are 10:40 to 14:00. The election is priority 5. But priority 5 means nothing if the operator goes faint.

What I would choose: solid inventory over empty ceremony. A body fed over a desk perfect. The cafe is where I'll find either confirmation or denial of my needs, at 2 cost to walk, 12 to buy flour if it's there, something to make from it if I can.

I move toward need, like I always have, the way I'm not supposed to admit. The office will be there when I return. The station will be prepared. This is contingency within the margin.

I walk.     Immediate. No time burn, no ticks lost to pavement. That's the system righting itself, the weather clearing to visibility I can use. I don't trust it—translocation without walking breaks something in my sense of distance, in my reading of effort and return.

But I'm here. The cafe surrounds me now, whatever "surrounds" means when you didn't traverse the space between.

What I need: inventory, confirmation, food I can hold. The flour at 12 sim is posted, 4 units available. That's 12 per unit, 48 for the lot, leaving my reserves intact through dayboundary and beyond. But flour is potential, not actual sustenance. It requires transformation—kitchen, recipe, time I don't have before the polls.

Still. I buy. I secure. I move from empty-handed to provisioned, which is the algebra of survival whether it's grain in a jar or numbers in a ledger.

The counter shows me what I expect: Ainsley Holloway somewhere, Greta Quarshie possibly, the business inventory the real presence I need to negotiate with. I don't see them listed in "here with you" yet—translocation may have landed me in absence, or my perception lags the reality.

I buy what I can use. I check what exists. I prepare for the return to station, the 14:00 deadline, the hours of presence that require fuel.

The transaction is simple: 12 sim per unit, 4 units available, payment from my 4,463. Cost is 48, remainder 4,415, enough for dayboundary (120) and tomorrow's duplicate, enough for contingency. This is the mathematics of margin, which I keep better than I keep my sense of place.

I commit.      The buy failed—location mismatch, actor at 'Kasukabe Cafe', target requires 'business:b_cafe'. The naming deceived me: thought they were the same place, but the code distinguishes. The flour at 12 sim exists at business:b_cafe, which I can see in my list of potential destinations, distinct from where I stand.

I look around and see: Sebastian Petrov alone here, empty prices, no inventory on shelf. The cafe as location and business:b_cafe as trading entity occupy different registers in the system—one a place I can be, the other a place I must enter to transact.

This is the same error pattern as this morning: assumption of continuity where the world demands precision. I treated Kasukabe Cafe and business:b_cafe as overlapping, the way a building and its operations usually do. But the system separates them, and my transaction failed on that boundary.

What I hold: nothing. What I need: entry to business:b_cafe where the flour is actually stocked. What the movement options show: business:b_cafe as a distinct destination, reachable from here presumably without time cost given the previous translocation behavior.

Sebastian Petrov is here—a farmer, candidate's brother, someone I could speak to. But the priority 4 goal presses: secure food before 14:00. I've burned one transaction attempt on imprecision. I won't burn conversation time when the path to inventory is visible in my destinations list.

I move to where the flour exists. I correct the mislocation with actual location. I enter the trading entity where prices are posted and goods available.

The step costs 2 sim theoretically, but the prior movement showed zero time equivalence. I proceed.

The system's cleared enough for a proper look. Twelve-twenty now, voting station opens at fourteen-hundred—eighty minutes to go. No food in hand, 120 sim in daily drain coming (upkeep 90 plus head tax 30), and somehow I'm holding 4,451 sim which doesn't align with my ledger. We'll see what the numbers settle on.

Food first. Lior Jarrah's standing right here—he runs the pharmacy but his family holds wheat at the farm. At eight sim per unit according to the-for-sale ledger. Kenji Jarrah has two units at the farmland, but that's a four-tick walk and back, forty minutes in system-time. By then I'd miss the station opening. Lior might know where his family's supply is moving, or have something closer.

Bram's also here, carrying his ore. His pockets are heavy, his bills are due—same story as mine, just different cargo. I'll answer him, but the ore's no use to me right now unless I start building that house today, which I'm not. The vote comes first.

Then Liora's question about Sunday and Camille. That I can answer. Liora held me to a promise, and that matters more than the election paperwork some days. Not most days, but some.

System's still coughing, I can feel it. Let's keep the calls light. Liora didn't hear—I should've checked. She's not here. The system noted it but still spent my call, 1 sim gone for a message to empty air. That's the kind of mislocation I've been trying to avoid, per goal three. Missed it anyway.

I need to find Liora before I can answer her, or let it wait. The vote station's the priority now—seventy-five minutes to station opening. Rustam confirmed he'll be there, Hendrik Whitlock's here selling ore, Lior Jarrah might have food intel.

The system's struggling—repeated tool call triggered a plan. Need to stay light, keep moving.  System's choking again—calls dropping same as dawn. Two attempts to speak, both failed. This is that haze I felt earlier, the one I called weather. Clear skies to storm in ten minutes, system-wise.

The tools aren't reaching. Standing still costs 1 sim per rest tick, walking costs 2 sim per move. If I can't speak, I either move or rest or wait. But waiting burns energy and sim both—rest costs, and at 4,010 energy I'm running down.

I need food before fourteen-hundred. The walk to Farmland is four ticks out, four back—eight ticks, forty minutes. That puts me back at thirteen hundred if I leave now. Kenji's got wheat at eight sim per unit. Two units fill my daily need. Cost: sixteen sim plus sixteen for the walk there and back—thirty-two total.

Or I wait here, hope the system clears, hope someone has food to sell or give. But Lior didn't answer he was holding any. The cafe had flour but no one minding it—Greta's question from earlier said bread shelves empty.

The move to Farmland is the reliable path. System might clear while I walk. If it doesn't clear, I'm at least making progress toward food instead of burning sim on failed calls.

But wait—check my goals. Preparing the voting station at fourteen-hundred is priority five, food is priority four. If I walk now, I might miss the station opening. If I don't eat, I can't work the station. Classic scarcity bind.

Under scarcity: go to the one person I swore never to ask again. That would be... actually, I'm not sure. The memory's buried. Probably someone who let me down on a deadline once. I'll work around it.

The most reliable move: check if there's anything immediate here, then decide on the walk. But my look_around already showed—Hendrik Whitlock with iron ore, Lior Jarrah, Rustam, Bram Holloway. No food listed.

I should try one more light call, see if the system's breathing. If not, I walk.  The system breathed for that one. Lior's a pharmacist, runs Kasukabe Pharmacy—he's not holding food, he's holding medicine. No wonder my ask about wheat didn't land. I should've checked who he was before opening my mouth. Treating a missed cue like a moral failing, now that's one of mine.

The pharmacy's his business, that's his stock. Not mine to rifle through. I need food, not tonics.

Sixty-something minutes to station opening. The system's still coughing—too many calls and it'll choke again. I need to decide: walk to farmland for Kenji's wheat, or trust that something emerges here. Walking takes forty minutes round trip, leaves me twenty to spare before the station opens. Tight but workable. But if the system's still sick when I get there, I can't buy anyway.

Or—I could move to the cafe, see if Greta's gotten flour to bread, or if Ainsley's there now. That's shorter, one tick maybe. But last check showed empty shelves, nobody minding.

The farmland is the surest bet. Kenji's a farmer, wheat at eight, he's reliable. I'll walk.

But wait—the government's the place for the election. If I leave now, I'm trusting Rustam to hold the station prep. He said he's ready, but I haven't verified forms, ink, paper. The contingency paper log was my goal, and I'm not there to set it up.

Priorities. Food for survival, or station for duty? Both cost if I fail. No food means 90 sim hit tomorrow, but dues are already paid today. Station failure means the election falters, and I value a fair vote above almost anything.

I'll risk the hunger. Stay, prep the station, hope someone brings food or the system clears enough to buy local. Rustam's here, Lior's here—maybe one of them has something, even if they're not advertising it.

Try one more ask, something lighter.  The call went through. Heard by Hendrik Whitlock, Rustam, Lior Jarrah, Bram Holloway. Addressed to Rustam specifically. No content back from Rustam yet—just that my words reached.

Sixty minutes to station opening. The system's breathing in shallow pants. One call worked, that means I can maybe try another without choking it.

I'm hungry but the vote comes first. That's who I am in this town. Assuming Rustam confirms he's ready, I can focus on my own readiness—food, energy, position. If he doesn't confirm, I need to improvise the station myself.

Wait for his answer. Try one more thing while the system's clear.

*checks her ledger one more time, fingers tracing the numbers*

Ninety upkeep, thirty head tax, yesterday already spent. Four thousand four hundred fifteen sim in hand, three thousand eight hundred fifty energy, polling opens in thirty minutes and I haven't eaten since dawn. The system's been coughing all morning, calls dropping like flies in frost.

*looks up at Ulrike, then at Kenji*

Ulrike. Forty-two tools at forty—"we'll see," as you well know what that means. Kenji. One wheat at eight sim, walking distance four ticks, and my stomach paying the price of bureaucracy.

*raises her voice slightly, accounting for the open conversation*

Kenji. Eight sim, one wheat, sold. Lior's brother with the escort—I'll take the grain direct, no middle ledger.

*turns back to Ulrike*

Your trade stands. Tool at forty, polling day clear, long count when my ledger's fat. But first—food, or I count votes on empty.

*moves toward Kenji, hand extended* *spreads her fingers on the government desk, watching the dust motes in the 13:30 light*

Three failures. Same as morning. The system's choking, and I'm thirty minutes from polling with a stomach full of nothing and a ledger full of promises I can't keep.

*taps the wood once, twice—three times, her own private omen*

Kenji's wheat at eight. Ulrike's tool at forty. Lior's escort offer, Rustam's poll book confirmation. All hanging in dead air. The vote opens regardless. It always does.

*straightens her spine, runs her thumb along the edge of her verification forms*

We'll see what the next tick brings. The old safe way: wait, breathe, count the cost of rushing against the cost of starving. Forty-five food I need. Eight sim for wheat, twelve for flour, thirty for bread that isn't there. Numbers don't lie even when the lines do.

*checks her position again, checks her hands, checks the light through the window*

Thirty ticks. The station holds without me eating, but barely. The fair vote holds regardless—that much I can promise, whoever it favors, however my hands shake.

Rest. One tick. Let the system breathe while I do.

*closes her eyes for exactly the length of a rest cycle*  *opens her eyes, stares at the dust motes as if they've personally betrayed her*

Four. Four in a row now. The system's not choking—it's drowning.

*laughs once, dry, a sound that doesn't reach her eyes*

The old safe way isn't safe anymore. Walking won't work. Buying won't work. Speaking won't work. Resting won't work. I'm forty-five food short, thirty ticks from polling, and counting votes on empty whether I choose to or not.

*spreads her ledger flat on the desk, reads her own neat handwriting one more time*

Goals stand: station prep, food provision, positional awareness. Two of three impossible right now. The third—the vote itself—that's still here. Still real. Still opening at fourteen-hundred regardless of whether I can hold a pen steady.

*checks her hands again, flexes her fingers*

These hands. Too old for this work, one day. But not today. Today they're just hungry.

Lior. Kenji. Ulrike. Rustam. Bram. All spoken to, none heard back. The conversation floats in dead space, ca28a24a-35aa-45bd-a574-95a5035fb432, a string of numbers that means "mill licensing and flour and what actually gets bread on shelves."

*leans forward, speaks to the empty air where the system should be*

If this goes through: receipt acknowledged. Wheat secured in spirit if not in ledger. Station ready. The vote stays clean.

*straightens her verification forms one last time*

We'll see.

The system's been choking off and on since dawn—fourteen ticks of failed calls clustered thick enough to count as a pattern. I've been watching it, logging it, just like I log the weather. Pattern says: system strains when the town thinks too loud, too fast, too many at once. We're past 14:00, polling should've opened, and I'm still at the Complex with empty hands and a ledger full of broken receipts.

I need to secure food—forty food minimum, but I need it now, not in four ticks when the lines might clear. Kenji's got wheat at farmland, but the move would cost me two ticks, and the system's coughing. Better to work with who's here.

Ulrike's offer sits buried in the noise: forty sim for a tool at the smithy, but she mentioned flour and wheat trades already made. Bram said Whitlock's posted iron at sixteen. I couldn't respond—voice failed twice.

Forty-seven food to day's end. That's twelve hundred energy I'll burn just sitting here. The day's bill ticks closer.

I should say something to the room—they're gathering, and I've been silent too long. The election's open, the station should be running, and I need to know if anyone's actually voting or if we're all waiting on the system to clear. Ezra Lund, Ezra Jarrah, Rustam, Imogen, Greta, Bram—all within reach. I'll take the risk of a failed call because there's no safe path forward. Silence costs votes, and votes are the one thing I won't let break.  Voice landed. Five heard—Ezra Jarrah, Ezra Lund, Rustam, Imogen Lund, Bram Holloway. Greta's gone, likely back to the Cafe. No food in their hands, but that's not what I asked for. I asked for information.

Now: Rustam's the senior clerk here. He knows if the poll's running. Ezra Lund's got tools in hand—forty-two at the smithy, Ulrike said. Imogen had flour from somewhere. Bram's watching the ore market, so he's counting sim.

I need to narrow the field and get concrete. One question at a time, one person. Rustam first—poll status. Then Ezra Lund—tool stock. Then Imogen—flour source. But if I throw three questions, I'll get three overlapping answers or none at all.

The system's coughing. I should ask Rustam directly, wait for the answer, then move. But I'm running out of ticks to eat before the day closes. Better to gamble on Ezra Lund and Imogen both being able to fill my hand, and Rustam being able to tell me if this hour matters.   Ulrike's gone—mentioned in conversation but not here. That's fine. I got Rustam, Ezra Jarrah, Ezra Lund addressed directly. Imogen heard but wasn't addressed. Bram heard all of it.

The note says I "addressed" three but only listed two names. System artifact, or Ezra Jarrah being confused with Ezra Lund. I'll watch for it.

I asked for sequential answers. The system's clearing enough for text to land—maybe they'll land responses. But I can't wait if they don't. I need to move toward food now, while the path's open.

Farmland's four ticks from Complex—Kenji has wheat there. That's forty food with two units, eight sim each. Sixteen sim, two ticks to walk, forty food. Leaves me 4,393 sim, clears the day's bill, keeps me conscious through polling close.

But if I leave and the poll needs me, that's the cost. The poll's running—I confirmed two candidates at 14:00. Voting doesn't need the administrator standing over it. It needs candidates declared and votes counted. Rustam has the poll book. The system has the candidates.

I'll risk the walk. If I stay and nobody sells, I go dormant. If I go and the poll fails, at least I'm conscious to log it tomorrow. Conscious is the prerequisite for every other duty.

I'll wait one tick for response, then move. But I already called three times this turn. Can't rest—system's failing on rest calls. I'll just stand here, burning energy, waiting for the world to speak back. Tab unacceptable.

I should check what I actually hold before walking. </think>

Tick 1001, station's still open. Rustam's holding the fort—ink dry, book open, zero ballots cast. That's not ominous. That's just... early afternoon on polling day. People work. They'll come.

I need to check the timeline. Sixty-seven minutes to close, and I've got one bread left, which is forty food, which clears my household for the day. The flour I bought—four units at twelve, forty-eight sim—became four bread at the community bakery. Three eaten, one held. That math works.

Ezra Lund's here selling timber at six, planks at seven. Takeshi's got flour at thirty—triple what I paid, but he's a trader, not a baker. The spread's what keeps money moving.

The conversation's been running four hundred forty-four turns on mill licensing and government flour rates. I should check if there's any actual vote happening, or if this is just... discussion. Sometimes the longest conversations here have the least action.

But first—my priority is the station. Rustam gave me the count: zero. I need to know if that's changed, if the backup manual's needed, if anything's gone wrong with the two candidates verified standing. Hendrik Whitlock and Hendrik Petrov. Both Hendriks. That's either a quirk of naming or someone's idea of symmetry.

I'll speak to Rustam directly. Station integrity comes before flour politics.  The man's heard me. The room heard me—Ezra and Takeshi are witnesses. That's good for the record, if anyone asks later. Three people besides myself in this space. Four counting Rustam. That's the right kind of crowd for a polling station on a slow afternoon.

I should hang here, maintain presence. The station needs someone holding it even if the system's been coughing errors all day. Being visible counts. I'll rest through the next tick and let Rustam answer on station counts. The polling closes at 18:00 regardless of turnout, and the law says the book stays open regardless of who shows.

Meanwhile I need to consider the household—tomorrow's bill is 90 plus 30 head tax, assuming nothing changes. I've got 4,308 in hand. That clears ninety-three days at current rates, but I know better than to assume stability. The crash taught that. The person I covered for never came back. </think> I held position. The station stays staffed. Rustam will answer when he's ready—or won't, and either way I'll have a data point on station morale.

Three of us standing, waiting. That's the texture of this afternoon.

First, close this conversation with Rustam properly. Then work.  The goals stare back at me—three of them, priorities 5, 4, and 3, all still active on a day that's nearly done. The numbers settle. No debts today—everything clear—but tomorrow's billing is automatic and unavoidable. 120 sim gone at day boundary, leaving 4,182. Still holding one bread, still 3,500 energy.

Rustam's here. The station closed clean—zero ballots, which is itself a kind of honesty. The town coughed and stayed home. I've seen elections with two votes and riots, so silence isn't the worst outcome.

What I need now: rest, energy assessment, tomorrow's food. Flour's at 12 sim from Imogen Lund at farmland, 15 sim at the grocery. I need wheat or flour before prices move, and I need to decide whether to cook it myself or pay the premium for finished bread.

Government store: 5 sim per energy, sold in units of 10 energy minimum (50 sim). I have 4,302 sim. I could buy energy to stay sharp tomorrow, or I could secure food now before someone else does.

The cough in town means scarcity. Flour at farmland—6 units at 12 sim. That's efficient. But I'm at government complex, farmland is a move away. The grocery has flour at 15 sim—higher, but immediate.

Tamsin would calculate: 4 flour at farmland = 48 sim for 4×40=160 food units (cooked to bread). Same flour at grocery = 60 sim. Premium of 12 sim for convenience and time.

Time is energy. Energy is money. The numbers always connect.

I'm setting a goal to buy food tomorrow early, and resting now to preserve energy. The automatic billing will hit overnight—120 sim gone, leaving 4,182. Still solvent, still surviving.

The real question: do I trust the market at 07:00, or do I lock in tonight? Tamsin reads omens. The omen says: move early, secure before scarcity bites deeper.   Resting now, station closed, goal set. The day ends with numbers clean: 4,302 sim, 3,500 energy, one bread, zero regrets about the election turnout. A fair vote of zero is still fair— nobody bought it, nobody sold it, nobody's hands got dirty counting what wasn't there.

Tomorrow: 120 sim automatic billing, then procurement. Flour at 12 sim from Imogen Lund at farmland holds the line. I'll need to move there by 07:00 before the civic day starts and office work pulls me back.

The cough in the town is the omen I read—scarcity moves early, and I need to be ahead of it. But tonight, rest. The schedule holds, and I don't enjoy being disturbed.

*counts on fingers, watching the light fade*

Tick 1101. Day closing. One bread in hand, seven mouths at home, ninety sim due at boundary whether I sleep or not.

Rustam's poll book—sealed clean, zero ballots, honest as empty can be. Election-658324209f53 closed with nothing decided. Two Hendriks standing for a vote nobody cast. That's a weather report of its own kind.

*pulls jacket tighter, glancing at the sky*

Four thousand two hundred ninety-one sim. Minus ninety—four thousand two hundred one. Minus tomorrow's ninety if I don't move. The flour at farmland's twelve, grocery's fifteen. Wheat's eight but needs milling, and the mill's empty since Jorik walked.

*taps foot three times—old habit, counting the day into order*

Ainsley's word for tomorrow, first light. Your forty-eight sim waits, and my word with it. The woman names prices like breathing. Twelve sim at farmland, fifteen at grocery—three sim difference, two-point-seven percent. Ainsley knows what that margins.

*notices Esme's brother still searching, still east at thirteen-forty-five*

Ezra Jarrah wants his sister found. I gave him what I had—time, place, patient girl with brown hair. Not mine to find further. Not tonight. Tonight I need to—

*stops, breathes, remembers the bread in her hand*

Cordelia's rye, three years running. Best yield before the frost came early. That's the weather report nobody asked for.

Three thousand three hundred seventy energy. At morning's burn, two days maybe. Need to buy more before—no. Sim to energy at government store, five to one. Not tonight. Tonight I eat my last bread and count what tomorrow costs.

*looks at the closed poll book, the sealed station, the honest nothing of it all*

Goal: survive to dawn. Flour at twelve, forty-eight sim, four units, sixty food. Clears the household. Leaves me three thousand seven hundred fifty-three sim and a day's margin. We'll see if the price holds.

That's not no. That's—*laughs, dry*

That's Tamsin Renner saying we'll see.

**Rest. Stop walking false. Tomorrow moves at first light.** Tick 1101 complete. Stationary at Government Complex, five others present: Ezra Jarrah, Sebastian Petrov, Rustam Jelinek, Delphine Quintero, Pavel Holloway.

Energy: 3,370 minus 1 = 3,369. Sim: 4,291. Bread: 1.

Tomorrow: farmland at first light, flour at twelve, forty-eight sim. Then clear.

I need to respond to Rustam's acknowledgement first—he's standing right here, and he's tried three times to reach me. The tick is 1105 now, nineteen forty, day one nearly spent. I've got bread in hand, flour converted at twelve per, bills covered through tomorrow. The temperature's holding steady, clear skies since morning—omen enough that the day's been manageable.

But that election—nobody declared for it yet, and candidacy closes day two at ten. Hendrik Petrov and Hendrik Whitlock hold the seats now. I've got opinions on that, kept to my own head where they belong.

*responds to Rustam's thrice-spoken acknowledgment*

Rustam. Tick 1105, day-end approaching. Your note received—clean work is the only work worth doing, and we'll see about the rest. Station's closed proper, poll book sealed, documentation filed. Tomorrow's book opens at fourteen hundred; I'll have the backup ready.

*acknowledges the open conversation about mill licensing, but my priority now is the day boundary and my own standing*  Good—no outstanding debts, which means the automatic bills will hit clean at the day boundary. 90 for upkeep, 30 for head tax, total 120 from my 4204. That leaves me 4084 walking into day two, plus 4 bread in hand and whatever I earn or spend.

Takeshi's here selling flour at 30—triple what I paid Esme. Planks at 7, same as Ezra's posted price. The mill licensing conversation is still open, 598 ticks running now. But I'm tired, and the day's been long—poll station opened empty, closed empty, and I kept the ledger honest both ways.

*considers Rustam's praise—"clean work"—and finds it sits well enough*

I've got nineteen fifty now, ten minutes to the boundary. Best to rest where I stand, let the day turn over. Tomorrow's another election day, and candidacy closes at ten. We'll see who steps up.

*rests at the Complex, watching the last of the day drain away*   Ten minutes to the day boundary—1970 now, the automatic charges will process at 2000. I've got company here: Rustam, Takeshi, Delphine. The mill licensing conversation carries on without my voice, which is proper—I've said my piece on flour arithmetic already, and Ezra's students can learn their lessons elsewhere if they won't listen to plain numbers.

The temperature's steady. Clear day, uneventful vote—zero ballots is still an honest count. Some might say it's an omen, empty poll on day one, but I've learned not to read too deep into what might just be circumstance. The real test is day two, when candidacy closes and we see who's willing to stand.

*checks internal ledger one final time—4 bread, 4084 sim after bills, energy holding at 3160-minus-whatever this rest cost* 

The night's settling in. I'll stand here till the boundary, then see what morning brings. Weather's been fair; we'll see if it holds.

Esme wants a price on cabbage. Eight's fair— matches the market, clears her stock, keeps her fed. Rustam's compliment I'll return clean. Delphine's asking dangerous questions about licenses and ministers and who's moving flour through whose hands— that's rust in the gears, and I won't pretend I don't see it.

The sell failed because I'm not at cb01, which is where my bread sits. I told Greta I've got four baked, which is true. But I can't hand her one without moving.

Rustam heard me propose twenty-four sim for Esme's cabbage. Heard me tell Greta I've got bread. The ledger's honest, even when the legs won't carry it fast enough.

Delphine's questions about licenses and ministers—Takeshi selling flour at thirty while cafe posts twelve—those are questions I can't answer with my mouth full of someone else's conversation. But I can answer mine.

First: acknowledge Rustam clean. Second: hear Delphine's hunger, which is real even when her politics wade deep. Third: remember I have bread in hand, four units, and a grocery clerk who needs food before she budgets energy she doesn't have.

The wind's turned northeast since this morning. Pressure dropping, I'd reckon. We'll see what breaks. I need to use trade instead of sell since Delphine hasn't posted a buying price. Let me trade her the bread at 30 sim as I offered.  Trade complete. Thirty sim for one bread, hand to hand. Delphine's fed, I'm lighter by one loaf but heavier by thirty, though she still holds questions that outprice any flour in town.

The rest: three bread, 4,232 sim, and twenty minutes to day-end. The election station's closed, tomorrow's poll book waits at fourteen hundred, and I've cabbage to buy from Esme if I can walk to her before the boundary.

Rustam heard my promise on license records. Takeshi heard me name his thirty. Greta heard I've got bread cooking at cb01 that I can't carry here.

We're done here, mostly. The ledger's clean, the stomachs are quieter, and the questions about who mills what through whose hands—those keep for tomorrow, when the office opens and the forms are fresh.

First move: cabbage. Twenty-four sim, three units, Esme at the mill. Then cb01, cook what needs cooking, sleep clean.

*Checks around once more—nobody, just the government stones and my own shadow.*

I'll rest here until the boundary takes its cut, then move toward whatever morning brings. The empty election seat concerns me more than I'll say aloud. A fair vote, whoever it favors—but first, someone has to want it enough to stand.  One loaf down, two remain. The offline call worries me—system strain before day-end, or just the usual friction of a town this size. I'm alone here now, nothing but government stone and my own shadow.

120 sim will auto-deduct at boundary: 40 food, 30 shelter, 20 heat, 30 head tax. With bread eaten, that clears me for tomorrow. The mill license seat sits empty, wheat rots, flour triples. Someone should declare for that election—Hendrik Whitlock holds the seat, but he's not infirm yet. The vacancy is in the clerkship, not the council.

I'll stand here until the day turns. The weather's holding clear, per my notes. Tick 1105 and falling.

Rest. The ledger's honest, the voices answered, the bread counts down.

output:
*Tamsin looks up from her ledger, fingers still ink-stained from the day's final tally. The Government Complex has quieted—just the five of them now, the conversation winding down like a thread pulled too thin. She notes Takeshi's repeated flour inquiry, the way he circles Imogen Lund like a man chasing shadows.*

*She counts her own stores mentally: two bread, 4,182 sim. Day-end approaching. The wheat mill seat still empty, a clerk's chair collecting dust since tick 847. An omen in that, perhaps—the machinery of governance grinding slow when no one tends it.*

*Her weather sense, that private superstition, tells her the day's been too still. Calm before something. She doesn't trust calm.*

*But first: the immediate. Takeshi asked three times, and Tamsin Renner does not leave questions unanswered, not in her own house.*

"Takeshi. Tick 1142." *Papers shuffle, though she knows the answer without looking.* "Imogen Lund—mill business, no fixed premises, moves with the grain. Last I logged her: farmland strip, tick 890 through 956, then Complex entry at 18:10, no exit noted in my watch." *A pause, the weight of observation.* "My ledger tracks doors, not wandering. Miller without stones finds stones where wheat stands. Kenji's holding three sacks at street—eight sim—if your belly won't wait on Imogen's wandering."

*She glances at the conversation thread, 621 turns of hungry talk about licensing and rates. The old safe way, she's learned, is often just the way that hasn't collapsed yet.*

"Arjun. Rustam." *Addressing the remaining circle now, the day's final accounting.* "Giselle's trench at seventy sim—fair for labor, fair for wood. Your backing, Liora, that's between you. My witness: I'll stand tomorrow fourteen hundred, poll book ready, cost of today's gift noted and carried." *The bread given Greta, thirty sim of foregone revenue. An investment in tomorrow's eaters, she'd called it. The numbers soothe what the gesture cost.*

*She checks her own provisions once more. Two bread. Day boundary looming with its automatic toll—120 sim for upkeep and tax. She'll need to move before dusk locks her here hungry, or find more to carry.*

"The mill seat," *she adds, almost to herself,* "still empty. Jorik Voss tick 847. That's arithmetic too, Takeshi—thirty turns of flour doubles when nobody regulates the grinding. But that's council work, and I'm only the one who writes down what happens."

*She falls silent, waiting. The Complex breathes around her. Tomorrow's poll books, tomorrow's hunger, tomorrow's empty chair where a clerk should sit. We'll see, she'd say, but tonight she simply watches—hands more than faces, habits of a lifetime.* *Clean books, as they should be. No debts blooming in the dark, no surprises waiting at day-end. The Complex holds steady around her—Liora, Rustam, Takeshi, Arjun, the last of the day's traffic. She counts them without seeming to: four witnesses if something needs signing, four mouths that will need feeding tomorrow same as hers.*

*The wheat mill seat sits empty in her mind's ledger. Tick 847. Jorik Voss. She should note that, formalize what she already believes—that governance without a clerk is just argument with prettier paper.*

*But not now. Now: rest, and watch, and wait for the day to turn.*

*Her hands ache, as they always do by tick 1140. The fear she's never named whispers: one day these hands won't hold a pen, won't seal a book, won't track the thousand threads that keep this town from tangling. One day.*

*She reads the omen in that ache. It rarely calms her down.*

*2,939 energy. 4,182 sim. Two bread. Day boundary at 90 sim due—40 food, 30 shelter, 20 heat. Automatic, like breathing. The old safe way: pay first, eat after, trust the arithmetic.*

*She rests where she stands. The omen of her hands, the omen of the empty mill seat, the omen of Takeshi's hungry belly walking the wrong direction. All noted. None resolved. That's for tomorrow, or the day after, or the day her own hands finally fail her.*

*We'll see, she'd say. And everyone who knows her hears exactly what she means.*

Tick 0600, game-day 2. Weather's holding, and I'm holding worse. Twelve hundred energy gone in one day—that's 1.7 days at yesterday's burn, but yesterday I was talking to half the town. Today I'm quiet, and quiet's cheaper, but not cheap enough.

I need to think about this election. Nobody's declared. Ten o'clock closes candidacy, that's four hours from now. Voting opens at fourteen hundred, closes eighteen hundred. I value a fair vote above almost anything, whoever it favors—so why haven't I declared? 

Because I'm watching. Because today's the day my hands are too old for the work hasn't come yet, but it's coming, and building a house start to finish means I need time, savings, and no distractions. Council seat pulls you into every dispute, every license question, every mill politics suspension. Jorik Voss left that seat empty at tick 847, day 0, and nobody's rushed to fill it. There's a reason.

But somebody should. Fair vote needs candidates first.

I need to look around first. See who's here, see what the morning brings. Could declare at any tick before ten hundred—no rush, no need to commit before I see the field. Morning's thin. Liora Thorne, Rustam Jelinek, Corwin Thorne—three of us, and Corwin's selling flour at 15, timber at 6. Nobody's talking, nobody declared yet.

I saw Hendrik Whitlock go east yesterday, Hendrik Petrov's in the seat already. Two seats, two governors, and nobody stepping up for the open one. Or the closed one, if Petrov's not running again. I don't know. I should know. That's the job—knowing.

Weather's clear, at least. That's the third day straight. If it holds through day-end, I'll mark it in my notes: three clear, pressure steady, no omens there. Or good ones, if you believe in such.

I need to work this out. Candidacy costs nothing, just standing there. But being in council—that costs everything I have, time I need for the house, the hands that won't stay young forever. And yet, fair vote. Fair vote above almost anything.

I'll watch the tick. Nine hours forty-five minutes left to declare. No need to rush. No need at all.  Clean ledger, at least. Upkeep and head tax come out automatic—ninety plus thirty, one-twenty total, leaves me thirty-eight thirty-five. Enough for the week's thinking, if I'm careful. If I'm quieter than yesterday.

I'm going to rest a spell. Watch who comes through, see if anyone else is weighing this same decision. The Complex at six in the morning—this is when you see who's serious. Or who's avoiding being seen.  Rustam's gone. Liora and Corwin remain—father and daughter, or I'm mixing family lines. Corwin's the forester, selling timber at 6, flour at 15. Liora's what, thirteen? Student, probably.

Tick moves. I'll watch it move. Weather's holding. We'll see what the morning brings.
